set.overview: The North Arete is a six-pitch rock line up the northern crest of Matterhorn Peak, the high point of the Sawtooth Ridge above Twin Lakes. The pitches wander along a fractured, broken arete with mostly moderate climbing at 5.4 to 5.6, and the crux is a corner near the top of the route that is wider than it looks. A short exposed traverse around a gendarme leads to second-class ground and the summit. It is a long alpine day, and many of the moves feel stiffer than the 5.7 grade suggests.
set.approach: Start from the Twin Lakes trailhead near Bridgeport, where the Horse Creek trail leaves from behind the RV park. Switchbacks climb to meadows near 8,100 ft, after which the trail fades into brush and talus crossings. At a col around 9,500 ft, leave the main trail on a use trail up a ridge to a lake just above 9,800 ft. From the lake, follow a slabby ridge onto the moraine and cross a short, nearly level stretch of glacier, then climb the loose sandy gully to the start of the route, a fractured ramp about 200 ft below the prow of the arete.
set.descent_text: The usual way down is the southeast slope toward Horse Creek, which avoids the glacier and loose rock of the approach. Boot-ski the sand to the Matterhorn Peak and Twin Peaks saddle, then pick up the faint use trail down the drainage, which is easy to lose among talus and snow patches. Allow more time than the map suggests for this section, since the trail is often hard to follow.
hazards: Loose sand and rock in the upper approach gully
Loose scree above the third-pitch mantle
Exposed traverse around a gendarme on the summit ridge
Faint, hard-to-follow trail on the descent through talus and snow patches

review.notes: Single trip account for this line (late September). Season skipped: no stated window. Gain/distance not in fill.

set.overview: Tower Peak is a rugged granite summit on the northern edge of Yosemite, reached only by a long backpack from Leavitt Meadows. The Northwest Chute is the class 3 finish: from the ridge above Tower Lake the route crosses onto the west face and follows a chute of firm rock directly to the summit block. The scrambling is short and easy for the grade, and the real commitment is the distance, roughly 15 miles each way, which most parties split over a camp near Tower Lake.
set.descent_text: Reverse the ascent: come down the chute and the ridge crest, taking the snowfield on its edge if it is still holding snow, and return to the camp at Tower Lake. From there retrace the Tower Lake trail to the junction in Upper Piute Meadows, then follow the West Walker River trail north through the meadows to Leavitt Meadows. Plan on the walk out taking most of a day.
hazards: Hard snowfields below the ridge in early morning, which are best passed on the rock beside them
Steep talus and friction slabs on the way to the ridge
Easy class 3 moves past a gendarme and in the upper chute

review.notes: Season skipped: two late-summer reports, no stated window.

set.overview: Black Hawk Mountain is a granite summit in the Emigrant Wilderness north of Sonora Pass, reached by a very long trail walk up the Summit Creek drainage. The route follows the trail through aspen, woodland and meadow to Lunch Meadow, then leaves it for a grassy valley and a class 2 climb to the east ridge and the summit. Nothing on the climb is technical, but the distance makes it a long day or an overnight trip.
set.approach: Drive Highway 108 toward Sonora Pass and turn to Kennedy Meadows Resort. The road is gated just past the resort, so park at the Forest Service trailhead about half a mile back and walk in on the dirt road, which becomes a trail into the Emigrant Wilderness. The trail follows the Stanislaus River past Relief Reservoir and then goes up Summit Creek, about 10 miles to Lunch Meadow. Cross the creek there and head up a grassy valley toward the east ridge.
hazards: A band of snow below the east ridge that can be hard and icy where it lies in shadow
Steep, slippery slopes of snow or loose rock near the top in late fall
Fast-moving fall storms that turn conditions wintry

evidence.fact: about 25 miles round trip; halved for one way (12.5 mi)

review.notes: Single report (late October 1999). Gain skipped: only a round-trip total of about 4,800 ft. Descent and season not stated, skipped.

set.overview: Leavitt Peak is a broad volcanic summit just north of Sonora Pass, and the walk to it is a class 1 outing on the Pacific Crest Trail and a use trail. The route crosses three prominent saddles on the PCT, then climbs the wide east slope and ridge on a well-worn path to the summit area. It is a straightforward half-day for a fit hiker, with open views over the Emigrant Wilderness and the Sierra crest.
set.approach: Park at the small lot at Sonora Pass on Highway 108 and join the Pacific Crest Trail heading south. The trail crosses three prominent saddles on its way toward the peak. East of the summit a use trail branches off the PCT, and a good path from there climbs the broad east slope and ridge to the top. Stay on the crest trail until that branch rather than leaving it early.
set.descent_text: Return the way you came: follow the use trail down the east slope and ridge to the Pacific Crest Trail, then walk the trail back north across the three saddles to the parking area at Sonora Pass. The descent is about as quick as the climb and needs no route-finding beyond finding the junction with the PCT.

evidence.fact: about 2,400 ft gain for the round trip
11.2 miles round trip; halved for one way (5.6 mi)

review.notes: One November report. Descent is simply the round trip back to the car (the page does not describe it separately). Hazards and season skipped: none stated on a page I opened.

set.approach: Start at the St. Marys Pass trailhead on the west side of Sonora Pass in the Stanislaus National Forest. The trail climbs through forest and then open tundra to the shoulder above St. Marys Pass. From there it runs mostly level for a couple of miles along the ridge until it ends at a cluster of white rock on Stanislaus Peak's east saddle. The climb up the south face begins at that saddle.
set.descent_text: Go back down the same way: descend the south face to the east saddle, then follow the ridge and trail to St. Marys Pass and the trailhead. Keep to the rim on the way down, since social trails branch off in many directions on the descent and can pull you onto loose slopes away from the main line.
hazards: Class 2 moves to get around the white rock at the saddle
Steep, loose social trail up the rim
Loose ground in the class 2 scrambling just below the summit
Many branching social trails on the descent

review.notes: Gain/distance skipped: the only figures found cover Stanislaus plus Sonora Peak. Season not stated.

set.overview: Disaster Peak is a modest summit in the Carson-Iceberg Wilderness, reached by a trail that starts near the end of Clark Fork Road. The southwest ridge route follows the trail past two meadows, leaves it at a faint branch and climbs cross-country over sage-covered slopes to the ridge, then finishes up a steep talus summit hump. The climbing is class 2, and the main difficulty is finding the faint, muddy trail and the point to leave it.
set.approach: Take Highway 108 east to the Clark Fork Road, which turns off about 18 miles east of Strawberry. Drive about 9 miles up this road to the trailhead on the left, a short way before the road ends. The trail starts well and crosses two meadows, then a faint branch leaves on the right after the small meadow. It grows obscure near a cliff, then climbs steeply. Near the 8,800 ft contour, leave the trail to the left and climb the sage hillside to the southwest ridge.
hazards: Slick mud on the steep, obscure section of the trail
Faint trail and a hard-to-find branch after the small meadow
Continuous snow cover on the ridge in late fall
Steep talus on the summit hump

review.notes: One early-November report. Descent, gain, distance not stated; season described only in words, skipped.

set.overview: Highland Peak is the high point of the Carson-Iceberg area near Ebbetts Pass, with a lower south summit and a slightly higher north summit. This route follows the Pacific Crest Trail into Noble Canyon, passes Noble Lake, then takes a steep use trail to the saddle and climbs class 2 volcanic sand to the top. It is a long but non-technical day, with loose footing as the main complaint.
set.approach: Park in the day-use lot at Ebbetts Pass, which has pit toilets and a short spur to the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT south with switchbacks, dropping several hundred feet into Noble Canyon, and reach Noble Lake after about 4 miles. A use trail branches off the PCT where the lake's inlet is and climbs steeply to the saddle connecting with Highland Peak. From the saddle it is roughly another mile and a half to the lower south summit, with the higher north summit about three quarters of a mile beyond.
hazards: Loose volcanic sand on most of the summit climb and on the way down
Faint trail that can disappear in wet meadows or snow patches
Snow patches on the trail near Noble Lake early in the season

review.notes: Single report, distance is the author's estimate. Gain skipped: only 1,700 ft from the saddle stated. Descent skipped: the report came back a different way. Season not stated.

set.overview: Mokelumne Peak is the high point of the northern Mokelumne Wilderness, a rounded summit reached from the Tanglefoot trailhead by a trail and a short cross-country stretch. The route dips into Tanglefoot Canyon, leaves the trail in open forest, then climbs through brush to a saddle and follows an easy ridge to the top. It is class 2, and the main task is navigation through forest and manzanita.
set.approach: Reach the Tanglefoot trailhead by dirt roads from Bear River Reservoir; the roads are confusing and a GPS helps. Hike the trail through Tanglefoot Canyon, down one side and up the other, passing a small lake. Where the forest opens up, leave the trail, pass south of the bump at 8,628 ft, and climb to the saddle between it and Mokelumne Peak, working around the brush. A grassy watercourse is one way up to the saddle, and the ridge from there to the summit is easy.
hazards: Dense forest with few landmarks makes it hard to find where to leave the trail
Thick manzanita brush on the climb to the saddle
Little water: one spring on the climb out of Tanglefoot Canyon

evidence.fact: about 13 miles round trip; halved (6.5 mi)

review.notes: Assumes the row's standard route is the Tanglefoot line. Descent not stated; season not stated (late September and early August reports).
